Prolonged QT interval has been reported in post-marketing cases, particularly in patients with overdoses, concurrent illnesses, or those taking drugs that cause electrolyte imbalances or prolong QT intervals. Close monitoring is advised in such cases. 2. Both quinidine and azithromycin are known to increase the QTc interval. Therapy should be modified, and patients should be closely monitored. 3. Azithromycin and quinine also increase the QTc interval. Therapy adjustments and close monitoring are recommended. 4. Co-administration of quizartinib and azithromycin can mutually enhance their effects on QTc prolongation. Therapy should be modified, and patients should be closely monitored. 5. When azithromycin is co-administered with QT-prolonging drugs, frequent ECG monitoring is necessary to assess cardiac risk. 6. Azithromycin increases the levels or effects of ranolazine via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Both drugs also prolong the QTc interval. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is required. 7. Azithromycin increases the levels or effects of repotrectinib via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Due to the serious risk, alternative drugs should be considered. 8. Azithromycin increases the toxicity of ribociclib by prolonging the QTc interval. Ribociclib also increases azithromycin toxicity. Alternative drugs should be used to avoid serious risks. 9. Azithromycin increases the toxicity of rifabutin by reducing its metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 10. Azithromycin increases the levels or effects of rifampin via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. 11. Azithromycin increases the levels of rifaximin via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 12. Rilpivirine increases the toxicity of azithromycin by prolonging the QTc interval. Caution and close monitoring are advised. Rilpivirine should be used cautiously with drugs that increase the risk of Torsades de Pointes. 13. Azithromycin increases the levels or effects of rimegepant via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Alternative drugs should be used due to serious risks. 14. Azithromycin increases the levels or effects of riociguat by reducing its metabolism. Alternative drugs should be used, and patients should be monitored for signs of hypotension. 15. Azithromycin and risperidone both prolong the QTc interval. The significance of this interaction is unknown, but caution and monitoring are advised. 16. Azithromycin increases the levels or effects of ritonavir via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. 17. Azithromycin increases the levels of rivaroxaban by affecting hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 metabolism. Patients with renal impairment may experience significant increases in rivaroxaban exposure, leading to a higher bleeding risk. Use rivaroxaban only if the benefits outweigh the risks, and monitor closely. 18. Azithromycin and romidepsin both prolong the QTc interval. Azithromycin also increases the levels or effects of romidepsin via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 19. Azithromycin increases the levels or effects of ruxolitinib by affecting hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 metabolism. The significance of this interaction is unknown, but caution is advised. 20. Azithromycin increases the toxicity of sertraline by prolonging the QTc interval. The significance of this interaction is unknown, but caution is advised. 21. Azithromycin and sevoflurane both prolong the QTc interval. Alternative drugs should be used due to serious risks. 22. Azithromycin increases the levels or effects of simvastatin by affecting hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. 23. Azithromycin and siponimod both prolong the QTc interval. Alternative drugs should be used due to serious risks. 24. Sodium bicarbonate decreases azithromycin levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Separate administration by at least 2 hours and monitor closely. 25. Sodium citrate/citric acid decreases azithromycin levels by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Separate administration by at least 2 hours and monitor closely. 26. Azithromycin decreases the effects of sodium picosulfate/magnesium oxide/anhydrous citric acid by altering metabolism. Co-administration with antibiotics reduces efficacy by altering colonic bacterial flora needed for drug activation. Caution and monitoring are advised. 27. Azithromycin increases the toxicity of solifenacin by prolonging the QTc interval. The significance of this interaction is unknown, but caution is advised. 28. Azithromycin and sotalol both prolong the QTc interval. Therapy should be modified, and patients should be closely monitored. 29. Azithromycin increases the toxicity of sunitinib by prolonging the QTc interval. The significance of this interaction is unknown, but caution is advised. 30. Azithromycin increases the levels or effects of tacrolimus via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Tacrolimus and azithromycin both prolong the QTc interval. Alternative drugs should be used due to serious risks. 31. Azithromycin increases the levels or effects of talazoparib via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Talazoparib is a P-glycoprotein substrate, and co-administration with P-gp inhibitors may increase systemic exposure. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 32. Azithromycin and telavancin both prolong the QTc interval. The significance of this interaction is unknown, but caution is advised. 33. Azithromycin decreases the effects of temocillin by pharmacodynamic antagonism. The significance of this interaction is unknown, but caution is advised. 34. Azithromycin increases the toxicity of tetrabenazine by prolonging the QTc interval. The significance of this interaction is unknown, but caution is advised. 35. Azithromycin decreases the levels or effects of thiamine by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. 36. Thioridazine and azithromycin both prolong the QTc interval. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 37. Azithromycin increases the toxicity of thiothixene by prolonging the QTc interval. The significance of this interaction is unknown, but caution is advised. 38. Inhaled tobramycin and azithromycin both increase nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Concurrent or sequential use should be avoided to reduce the risk of ototoxicity. Therapy should be modified, and patients should be closely monitored. 39. Azithromycin increases the levels or effects of tolvaptan via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. 40. Azithromycin increases the levels or effects of topotecan via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Alternative drugs should be used due to serious risks. For oral topotecan, avoid co-administration with P-gp inhibitors. The interaction with IV topotecan may be less severe but still clinically significant. 41. Azithromycin increases the levels of toremifene by reducing its metabolism. Concurrent use of toremifene with QT-prolonging agents should be avoided. If co-administration is necessary, toremifene should be interrupted, or patients should be closely monitored with ECGs. 42. Trazodone and azithromycin both prolong the QTc interval. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 43. Trifluoperazine and azithromycin both prolong the QTc interval. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 44. Azithromycin and trimethoprim both prolong the QTc interval. The significance of this interaction is unknown, but caution is advised. 45. Azithromycin and trimipramine both prolong the QTc interval. Azithromycin also increases the toxicity of trimipramine. The significance of this interaction is unknown, but caution is advised. 46. Triptorelin increases the toxicity of azithromycin by prolonging the QTc interval, increasing the risk of Torsades de Pointes. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 47. Azithromycin and tropisetron both prolong the QTc interval. The significance of this interaction is unknown, but caution is advised. 48. Azithromycin decreases the effects of the live typhoid vaccine by pharmacodynamic antagonism. Co-administration is contraindicated. Wait until antibiotic therapy is complete before administering the live bacterial vaccine. 49. Azithromycin increases the toxicity of umeclidinium bromide/vilanterol inhaled by prolonging the QTc interval. Alternative drugs should be used due to serious risks. Extreme caution is advised when co-administering vilanterol with QT-prolonging drugs, as adrenergic agonist effects on the cardiovascular system may be potentiated. 50. Valbenazine and azithromycin both prolong the QTc interval. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 51. Azithromycin and vandetanib both increase each other’s toxicity by prolonging the QTc interval. Alternative drugs should be used due to serious risks. Avoid co-administration with QT-prolonging drugs. If necessary, frequent ECG monitoring is recommended. 52. Azithromycin increases the toxicity of vardenafil by prolonging the QTc interval. The significance of this interaction is unknown, but caution is advised. 53. Vemurafenib and azithromycin both prolong the QTc interval. Alternative drugs should be used due to serious risks. Concomitant use of vemurafenib with QT-prolonging drugs is not recommended. 54. Azithromycin increases the levels or effects of venetoclax via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Alternative drugs should be used due to serious risks. If a P-gp inhibitor must be used, reduce the venetoclax dose by at least 50% and monitor closely for signs of toxicity. 55. Azithromycin and venlafaxine both prolong the QTc interval. The significance of this interaction is unknown, but caution is advised. 56. Azithromycin increases the levels or effects of verapamil via P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. 57. Azithromycin increases the toxicity of vilanterol/fluticasone furoate inhaled by prolonging the QTc interval. Alternative drugs should be used due to serious risks. Extreme caution is advised when co-administering vilanterol with QT-prolonging drugs, as adrenergic agonist effects on the cardiovascular system may be potentiated. 58. Voclosporin and azithromycin both increase each other’s effects by prolonging the QTc interval. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 59. Azithromycin and voriconazole both prolong the QTc interval. The significance of this interaction is unknown, but caution is advised. 60. Azithromycin increases the toxicity of vorinostat by prolonging the QTc interval. The significance of this interaction is unknown, but caution is advised. 61. Azithromycin increases the toxicity of warfarin by enhancing anticoagulation. Post-marketing reports suggest that azithromycin may potentiate the effects of oral warfarin, but it does not appear to alter prothrombin time. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. 62. Azithromycin and ziprasidone both prolong the QTc interval. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 63. Elevated ALT, AST, and creatinine levels have been reported in 4-6% of cases, while elevated LDH and bilirubin levels occur in 1-3%. Other adverse effects include dyspepsia, flatulence, mucositis, oral moniliasis, gastritis, headache, somnolence, bronchospasm, taste perversion, leukopenia, neutropenia, decreased platelet count, and elevated serum alkaline phosphatase. 64. Allergic reactions such as arthralgia, edema, urticaria, and angioedema have been reported. Cardiovascular effects include arrhythmias (e.g., ventricular tachycardia), hypotension, QT prolongation, Torsades de Pointes, and cardiovascular death. 65. Gastrointestinal effects include anorexia, constipation, dyspepsia, flatulence, vomiting/diarrhea, pseudomembranous colitis, pancreatitis, oral candidiasis, pyloric stenosis, and reports of tongue discoloration. 66. General effects include asthenia, paresthesia, fatigue, malaise, and anaphylaxis (including fatalities). Genitourinary effects include interstitial nephritis, acute renal failure, and vaginitis. 67. Hematopoietic effects include thrombocytopenia. Liver and biliary effects include abnormal liver function, hepatitis, cholestatic jaundice, hepatic necrosis, and hepatic failure, some of which have resulted in death. Discontinue treatment immediately if signs of hepatitis occur. 68. Nervous system effects include convulsions, dizziness/vertigo, headache, somnolence, hyperactivity, nervousness, agitation, and syncope. Psychiatric effects include aggressive reactions and anxiety. 69. Skin reactions include pruritus and serious skin reactions such as erythema multiforme, acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP), Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, and drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS). 70. Special senses effects include hearing disturbances (e.g., hearing loss, deafness, tinnitus) and reports of taste/smell perversion or loss. 71. Hypersensitivity to azithromycin, erythromycin, macrolides, or ketolides is contraindicated. A history of cholestatic jaundice or hepatic dysfunction associated with prior azithromycin use is also contraindicated. 72. Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS) has been reported. Parents and caregivers should be advised to monitor for vomiting or irritability with feeding. 73. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported, ranging from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, discontinue ongoing antibacterial use not directed against C. difficile and initiate appropriate management. 74. Exacerbations of myasthenia gravis symptoms and new-onset myasthenic syndrome have been reported. 75. Antibacterial agents used to treat nongonococcal urethritis may mask or delay symptoms of incubating syphilis. Patients with sexually transmitted urethritis or cervicitis should undergo serologic testing for syphilis and appropriate testing for gonorrhea at diagnosis. If infection is confirmed, initiate appropriate therapy and follow-up testing. 76. Local IV site reactions have been reported with IV azithromycin. 77. Prescribing azithromycin in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of drug-resistant bacteria development. 78. Available data on azithromycin use in pregnant women have not identified any drug-associated risks for major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. 79. Azithromycin is present in human milk. Non-serious adverse reactions have been reported in breastfed infants after maternal administration. No data are available on the effects of azithromycin on milk production. Consider the developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding along with the mother’s clinical need for azithromycin and any potential adverse effects on the breastfed infant.
